question: Psychologist Robin Hogarth contrasts 'kind' and 'wicked' learning environments. What makes one wicked?
options: Feedback is late, rare or misleading
answer: Feedback that is late, rare or misleading, so experience teaches the wrong lessons. Chess and golf are kind: clear rules, quick and accurate feedback, so practice makes perfect. Much of life, from medicine to business, is wicked, and there Epstein argues broad experience beats narrow repetition.
move: Ask whether your experience gets quick, honest feedback before trusting it.
trap: 'Nobody keeps score': wicked worlds keep score, just unreliably.
simply: In darts, you see right away if you hit the target, so you improve. In some jobs you never find out if you were right, so practice can teach you wrong.
why: Long experience feels like expertise, but in fields with poor feedback it may just be confidence. Seeking honest, fast feedback is the remedy.
reference: David Epstein, Range: Why Generalists Triumph in a Specialized World (Riverhead, 2019), ch. 1
